q: What are the most common wilderness medical emergencies?
How do I treat a severe wound in a survival situation?
What is direct pressure and when is it used?
How do I apply a tourniquet correctly?
What is a pressure bandage and how do I make one?
How do I clean and dress a wound in the wilderness?
What are signs of wound infection and how do I treat them?
What supplies do I need for wound care in a first aid kit?
a: The most common wilderness medical emergencies include lacerations and puncture wounds, fractures and sprains, burns, hypothermia and hyperthermia, dehydration, and allergic reactions—with bleeding being the most immediately life-threatening. For severe bleeding, apply direct pressure to the wound with a sterile gauze pad or any clean cloth, maintaining firm, continuous pressure for a full 10-15 minutes without lifting to check if bleeding has stopped (lifting disrupts clot formation). A tourniquet should be used only for life-threatening extremity bleeding that cannot be controlled by direct pressure—place it 2-3 inches above the wound (not over a joint), tighten until bleeding stops, note the time of application, and never remove it once applied (this should be done by a medical professional). Wound cleaning in the wilderness should use clean water (purified if available), with irrigation from a syringe or water bottle to flush debris from the wound, followed by gentle cleaning around (not in) the wound with soap and water. Signs of wound infection developing in the field include increasing pain, redness spreading from the wound, warmth, swelling, red streaks extending from the wound (lymphangitis), pus or cloudy discharge, fever, and chills—treatment includes keeping the wound clean, applying antibiotic ointment if available, changing dressings regularly, and beginning evacuation planning as systemic infections can progress rapidly without proper antibiotics.

q: How do I treat fractures and sprains in the wilderness?
How do I splint a broken bone in the wilderness?
What is RICE treatment for sprains?
How do I make a splint from natural materials?
How do I treat a suspected spinal injury?
What are SAM splints and how are they used?
How do I treat a dislocated joint in the field?
When should I evacuate for a fracture or dislocation?
a: Fracture and sprain management in the wilderness follows the RICE protocol: Rest (stop using the injured limb), Ice (apply a cold pack or snow in a cloth for 20 minutes every 2 hours), Compression (wrap with an elastic bandage from below the injury upward, firm but not so tight that it causes numbness or discoloration), and Elevation (keep the injured limb raised above heart level to reduce swelling). Splinting immobilizes a suspected fracture with the joint above and below the break immobilized—use a SAM splint (a moldable aluminum and foam splint that can be shaped to any limb) or improvise with natural materials (straight branches, rolled-up sleeping pad, trekking poles, or even the opposite leg for a lower extremity fracture), padding the splint with clothing or soft materials, and securing it with bandages, tape, or paracord above and below the injury. For a suspected spinal injury (from a high-impact fall, diving accident, or vehicle crash)—do not move the patient unless they are in immediate danger (fire, flooding, rockfall), maintain manual stabilization of the head and neck in neutral alignment, and wait for professional evacuation with a backboard or equivalent rigid support. Dislocated joints (especially shoulder, finger, and patella) can sometimes be reduced in the field using gentle, steady traction along the limb's axis with muscle relaxation—but only if you are trained in the specific reduction technique and there is no suspected fracture. All fractures, dislocations that cannot be reduced, injuries with neurological deficits (numbness, weakness, loss of pulse), and suspected spinal injuries require urgent evacuation.

q: How do I treat hypothermia in the wilderness?
What are the stages of hypothermia?
How do I prevent hypothermia in cold weather?
What is the difference between hypothermia and frostbite?
How do I treat frostbite in the field?
What are the signs of hypothermia in a companion?
How do I rewarm a hypothermic person safely?
What should I NOT do when treating hypothermia?
a: Hypothermia occurs when the body loses heat faster than it can produce it, with core temperature dropping below 95°F (35°C)—stages progress from mild (shivering, cold and pale skin, apathy, loss of fine motor coordination) to moderate (violent shivering or shivering stopping, confusion, slurred speech, irrational behavior, inability to stand or walk) to severe (unconsciousness, no visible shivering, slow and shallow breathing, apparent death). Treatment for mild hypothermia: remove wet clothing, insulate the person from the ground, provide warm drinks (non-alcoholic, non-caffeinated), apply external heat sources (hot water bottles wrapped in cloth, chemical heat packs, body-to-body contact in a sleeping bag) to the torso (armpits, chest, and groin—not arms and legs, because warming extremities first can cause cold blood to rush to the heart and trigger cardiac arrest). For moderate to severe hypothermia, handle the patient very gently (rough movement can cause cardiac arrest), do not give food or drink to an unconscious person, and begin active rewarming with warm (not hot) water bottles and thermal blankets while evacuating as soon as possible. Frostbite is tissue freezing from extreme cold exposure—rewarm frozen tissue only if there is no risk of refreezing (refreeze causes worse damage), using warm water (100-105°F, not hot) for 30-45 minutes, and never rub or massage frostbitten tissue (this causes ice crystals to damage cells). Prevention is critical: stay dry, layer clothing with wicking base layer, insulating mid-layer, and windproof outer layer, eat frequently for metabolic heat production, and recognize the 'umbles' (stumbles, mumbles, fumbles, grumbles) as early signs of hypothermia in yourself and companions.

q: How do I treat burns in the wilderness?
What are the degrees of burn severity?
How do I treat a first-degree burn in the field?
How do I treat a second-degree or third-degree burn?
What is the rule of nines for burn assessment?
What should I NOT put on a burn?
How do I prevent burn infection in the wilderness?
a: Burn severity is classified by degree: first-degree burns (red, painful, no blisters—like sunburn) damage only the epidermis and heal without scarring; second-degree burns (red, blistered, swollen, extremely painful) damage both epidermis and dermis; third-degree burns (white, charred, leathery, painless due to nerve destruction) penetrate all skin layers and require urgent evacuation. First-degree burn treatment in the wilderness: cool the burn immediately with clean, cool water (not ice—this can cause frostbite on the damaged tissue) for 10-15 minutes, then apply aloe vera gel or a moisturizing burn cream if available, and keep the area clean and covered from sunlight. For second-degree burns with intact blisters: cool with water, do NOT pop blisters (the intact skin is a natural sterile barrier against infection), cover loosely with a sterile non-stick dressing, and monitor for infection. For third-degree burns: remove any clothing not stuck to the burn, cover with a sterile or clean non-stick dressing, do not apply any creams or ointments, and evacuate immediately. Never put butter, oil, toothpaste, or ice directly on a burn—these home remedies trap heat, introduce bacteria, or cause additional tissue damage. The rule of nines estimates burn size for fluid replacement decisions: each arm is 9% of body surface area, each leg 18%, front torso 18%, back torso 18%, head and neck 9%, and perineum 1%—burns covering more than 15% of body surface area require urgent evacuation and IV fluid resuscitation.

q: What are heat-related emergencies and how do I treat them?
What is heat exhaustion vs heat stroke?
How do I treat heat exhaustion in the wilderness?
What are the signs of heat stroke and why is it an emergency?
How do I cool someone with heat stroke?
How do I prevent dehydration in hot environments?
What are heat cramps and how are they treated?
How much water do I need in hot weather?
a: Heat emergencies range from mild (heat cramps) to moderate (heat exhaustion) to life-threatening (heat stroke). Heat cramps are painful muscle spasms (usually in legs, arms, or abdomen) caused by electrolyte depletion from sweating—treatment includes rest in shade, stretching the cramped muscle, and drinking electrolyte solution or salted water. Heat exhaustion symptoms include heavy sweating, cold and clammy pale skin, weak pulse, nausea, dizziness, headache, and fainting—treatment involves moving to shade or a cool area, removing excess clothing, lying down with feet elevated, drinking cool water with electrolytes, and applying cool wet cloths to the neck, armpits, and groin (heat-exchange areas with major blood vessels near the skin surface). Heat stroke is a medical emergency where the body's temperature regulation fails, core temperature rises above 104°F (40°C), and sweating stops (hot, red, dry skin)—symptoms include confusion, seizures, loss of consciousness, rapid strong pulse, and high body temperature. Treatment for heat stroke requires aggressive cooling: move to shade, remove clothing, pour cool water over the person (especially the head, torso, and groin), fan vigorously, apply ice packs to armpits, groin, and the back of the neck, and evacuate immediately—without aggressive treatment, heat stroke can cause permanent organ damage or death within minutes. Prevention in hot environments: drink 4-8 ounces of water every 15-20 minutes during activity, supplement with electrolyte solutions after 2+ hours of sweating, wear light-colored loose clothing and a wide-brimmed hat, rest in shade during peak heat (10 AM - 4 PM), and monitor urine color as a hydration indicator (pale yellow = hydrated, dark yellow/amber = dehydrated).
